title: RIDDOR & reporting incidents
blurb: Which accidents, diseases and dangerous occurrences must be reported to HSE, how quickly, and why near misses matter too.
question: A dental nurse slips on a wet floor in the decontamination room, breaks her wrist and is taken to A&E. The practice manager asks you whether this has to be reported to anyone outside the practice, and how quickly. What is the answer?

teach.body: Every accident at work should be recorded in the practice accident book and investigated. A smaller group of serious incidents must also be reported to the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) under the Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013 (RIDDOR). The duty to report falls on the 'responsible person', usually the employer or practice owner. Reports are made to HSE online, with a telephone route for fatal and specified injuries.

Dental example
rows: Nurse fractures a wrist in a slip
Visitor trips, goes straight to A&E
Sharps injury from a known BBV source
teach.caption: A non-worker (patient or visitor) injury is reportable when it arises from a work activity and they are taken from the scene directly to hospital for treatment.

steps.label: Make the area safe
steps.sub: Stop it happening to anyone else

teach.body: These are the serious injuries to workers that are reportable straight away: fractures (other than to fingers, thumbs and toes); amputations; permanent loss or reduction of sight; crush injuries to the head or torso causing internal damage; serious burns (over 10% of the body, or damaging the eyes, breathing or vital organs); scalpings needing hospital treatment; loss of consciousness from a head injury or asphyxia; and injuries in an enclosed space causing heat illness or hypothermia, or needing resuscitation or more than 24 hours in hospital.

items.label: Over-7-day injuries
items.sub: From the day of the accident

items.label: Occupational diseases
items.sub: Once a doctor's written diagnosis is received

teach.caption: Counting the 7 days: don't count the day of the accident, but do count weekends and rest days. Over-3-day injuries must be recorded in the accident book but are only reported to HSE once they pass 7 days.

root.label: Sharps injury
root.sub: Always: first aid, record, occupational health

teach.caption: BBV = blood-borne virus such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV.

teach.body: Reportable diseases include occupational dermatitis and occupational asthma (both linked to gloves and chemicals in dentistry), carpal tunnel syndrome, tendonitis of the hand or forearm, hand-arm vibration syndrome, occupational cancers, and diseases caused by exposure to a biological agent. Dangerous occurrences are specified near misses with high potential for harm, such as a pressure vessel (compressor or autoclave) bursting, an electrical short circuit causing a fire, or release of a dangerous biological agent.

rows.label: Nurse fractures wrist slipping on a wet floor
Minor cut, back at work the same day
Tray nearly falls off the bracket table
Faulty medical device harms a patient

teach.note: Different events go through different systems. Your job is to report everything internally; the responsible person makes the RIDDOR report.

teach.body: A near miss is an event that could have caused harm but didn't, such as a cable that nearly trips someone. Most near misses aren't RIDDOR reportable, but recording them and discussing them at practice meetings lets the team fix the cause before someone is hurt. Near-miss reporting is about learning from warnings, not about blaming people.

teach.text: Over-3-day injury = RECORD it. Over-7-day injury = REPORT it to HSE within 15 days. And a fracture of a finger, thumb or toe is NOT a specified injury (though it may become reportable as an over-7-day injury).

items: Record every accident; RIDDOR 2013 requires reporting the serious ones to HSE.
Reportable: deaths, specified injuries, over-7-day injuries, non-workers taken to hospital, occupational diseases, dangerous occurrences.
Deaths, specified injuries and dangerous occurrences: notify without delay, report within 10 days.
Over-7-day injuries: within 15 days. Diseases: once diagnosed in writing.
Sharps injury is reportable only if the source is known to carry a BBV (or infection follows).
Report near misses internally so the team can learn and prevent harm.

summary: You can now tell an incident that just needs recording from one that must be reported to HSE under RIDDOR, list the reportable categories, give the reporting timescales, apply the rules to sharps injuries, and explain why near-miss reporting matters.

A.q: A dental nurse slips on a wet floor at work and fractures her wrist. Under RIDDOR this is:
options: Not reportable, as it was an accident
Reportable only if she is off work for 7 days
A specified injury, reportable without delay
Reportable only if a patient saw it happen
A.why: A fracture other than to a finger, thumb or toe is a specified injury and must be notified to HSE without delay.

whyNot.0: Accidents are exactly what RIDDOR covers.
whyNot.1: The 7-day rule applies to injuries that aren't specified injuries; a wrist fracture is reportable anyway.
whyNot.3: Witnesses have nothing to do with whether an injury is reportable.

A.q: Which event is most suitable for recording through the practice's workplace incident system?
options: A patient complaining about waiting times
A delivery arriving later than scheduled
A staff member slipping on spilt water
A stock item running low unexpectedly
A.why: A slip at work is a workplace incident that should be recorded and investigated.

whyNot.0: Complaints go through the complaints procedure.
whyNot.1: A late delivery is a supply issue, not a safety incident.
whyNot.3: Low stock is a stock-control issue.

A.q: Within what time must an over-7-day injury to a worker be reported to HSE?
options: Within 24 hours of the accident
Within 15 days of the accident
Within 3 months of the accident
Only if HSE asks for it
A.why: Over-7-day incapacitation injuries must be reported within 15 days of the accident.

whyNot.0: There is no 24-hour deadline for over-7-day injuries.
whyNot.2: Three months is far too late.
whyNot.3: Reporting is a legal duty; HSE does not have to ask.

B.q: A nurse sustains a needlestick injury from a patient known to have hepatitis C. How is this classed under RIDDOR?
options: A dangerous occurrence
A specified injury
Not reportable at all
An over-3-day injury
B.why: A sharps injury from a source known to be infected with a blood-borne virus is reportable as a dangerous occurrence.

whyNot.1: A needlestick is not in the list of specified injuries.
whyNot.2: Because the source is known to be infected, it IS reportable.
whyNot.3: Over-3-day injuries are about time off work and are recorded, not reported.

B.q: Who has the legal duty to make a RIDDOR report?
options: The injured member of staff
The responsible person (the employer)
Any colleague who witnessed it
The most senior GDC registrant on duty that day
B.why: RIDDOR places the duty on the 'responsible person', usually the employer or person in control of the premises.

whyNot.0: The injured person should report internally, but the RIDDOR duty is not theirs.
whyNot.2: Witnesses provide information; they don't make the RIDDOR report.
whyNot.3: GDC registration doesn't create the RIDDOR duty.

B.q: The team is discussing last month's incidents. What is the main value of near-miss reporting?
options: It shows who was responsible
It proves the controls are adequate
It replaces the need for risk assessment
It helps prevent future harm by learning
B.why: Near misses are warnings. Recording and discussing them lets the team fix causes before someone is hurt.

whyNot.0: Near-miss reporting is about learning, not blame.
whyNot.1: A near miss suggests the controls may NOT be adequate.
whyNot.2: Near misses feed into risk assessment; they don't replace it.

C.q: Which of these is NOT a specified injury under RIDDOR?
options: A fractured arm
A fractured finger
Loss of consciousness from a head injury
Permanent loss of sight in one eye
C.why: Fractures to fingers, thumbs and toes are excluded from the specified injury list.

whyNot.0: A fractured arm is a specified injury.
whyNot.2: Loss of consciousness caused by a head injury is a specified injury.
whyNot.3: Permanent loss or reduction of sight is a specified injury.

C.q: A nurse hurts her back lifting a box and is off normal duties for five days. What must happen?
options: Report it to HSE within 10 days
Report it to HSE without delay
Nothing, as it was under a week
Record it in the accident book
C.why: Over-3-day injuries must be recorded but are only reported to HSE if incapacity lasts more than seven days.

whyNot.0: Five days does not reach the over-7-day reporting threshold.
whyNot.1: It is not a specified injury, so immediate notification isn't required.
whyNot.2: It must still be recorded, as it is over three days.

C.q: A dental nurse is diagnosed in writing by her GP with occupational dermatitis from glove use. What applies?
options: Report to HSE once the diagnosis is received
Record it, but skin conditions are never reportable
Report only if she leaves her job
Report only if a patient is affected
C.why: Occupational dermatitis is a reportable disease once the responsible person receives a written diagnosis linking it to work.

whyNot.1: Occupational dermatitis is on the list of reportable diseases.
whyNot.2: Leaving the job is irrelevant to the reporting duty.
whyNot.3: The disease affects the worker; patients are not part of the test.

reteach.title: The accident book is the diary, RIDDOR is the phone call
reteach.question: Imagine the accident book as the practice diary and a RIDDOR report as a phone call to HSE. When do you only write in the diary, and when must you also pick up the phone?

blocks.h: Diary for everything, phone for the serious
blocks.body: Every accident goes in the diary. You pick up the phone to HSE (or report online) only for the serious ones: a death, a big injury like a broken arm, someone off work for more than a week, a visitor rushed to hospital, a work-caused disease, or a dangerous near miss such as a needlestick from a patient known to have a blood-borne virus.

steps.label: Is it on the reportable list?
steps.sub: Specified, over-7-day, disease, dangerous occurrence, non-worker to hospital

steps.label: Yes: report to HSE
steps.sub: And always record in the accident book

blocks.text: Three days off = write it down. More than seven days off = phone HSE (within 15 days).

explain.body: All accidents are recorded in the accident book. RIDDOR reporting to HSE is only for specific serious incidents, and it is the responsible person's duty.

test.q: A nurse cuts her hand slightly on a tray edge and carries on working. What is needed?
options: A RIDDOR report within 15 days
An entry in the accident book
A RIDDOR report without delay
A report to the GDC
test.why: A minor injury with no time off is recorded internally but is not reportable to HSE.

whyNot.0: The 15-day deadline is for over-7-day injuries.
whyNot.2: Immediate notification is for deaths, specified injuries and dangerous occurrences.
whyNot.3: The GDC regulates professionals; it doesn't receive accident reports.

explain.body: Specified injuries include fractures (not fingers, thumbs or toes), amputations, loss of sight, serious burns and loss of consciousness from a head injury. Over-7-day injuries keep a worker off normal duties for more than seven days, not counting the day of the accident.

test.q: When counting an over-7-day injury, which days are included?
options: Working days only, not weekends
Weekends and rest days, not the accident day
The day of the accident, plus working days only
Only days spent in hospital
test.why: Don't count the day of the accident, but do count weekends and rest days.

whyNot.0: Weekends and rest days are included.
whyNot.2: The day of the accident is not counted.
whyNot.3: Incapacity for normal work counts, wherever the person is.

explain.body: Occupational diseases are reported once a doctor's written diagnosis is received: for example occupational dermatitis or asthma, or carpal tunnel syndrome. Dangerous occurrences are listed near misses with high potential for harm, such as an autoclave bursting or a sharps injury from a known BBV-positive source.

test.q: A practice autoclave's pressure vessel bursts but nobody is hurt. Under RIDDOR this is:
options: Not reportable as no one was hurt
A specified injury
A dangerous occurrence
An occupational disease
test.why: Failure of a pressure system is a listed dangerous occurrence, reportable even when nobody is injured.

whyNot.0: Dangerous occurrences are reportable precisely because of their potential for harm.
whyNot.3: This is an event, not a disease.

explain.body: A near miss could have caused harm but didn't. It goes in the practice's internal log and is discussed so the cause is fixed. Most aren't RIDDOR reportable, unless they are on the dangerous occurrence list.

test.q: A colleague nearly trips over a trailing suction hose but doesn't fall. What should you do?
options: Report it as a near miss and fix the hazard
Report it to HSE under RIDDOR as a dangerous occurrence
Do nothing, as no one was hurt
Record it only if it happens again
test.why: Near misses should be recorded internally and the hazard removed, so it doesn't cause harm next time.

whyNot.1: This kind of near miss is not RIDDOR reportable.
whyNot.2: Ignoring it leaves the hazard in place.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a repeat risks an injury.
